intro: Mail carriers manage time, routes and the public every day, skills that fit transport and screening work. The closest of the 25 careers below is Bus Drivers, Transit and Intercity, with a 69% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $59,050, about 2% less than the $60,550 carriers earn.
why_it_works: Delivering a route means planning stops, keeping a schedule and dealing politely with hundreds of people. O*NET rates social perceptiveness at 3 out of 5 for carriers and time management at 2.88. Those habits match bus driving, airline cabin crew and airport screening. Every top 10 match needs no new schooling. To earn more, carriers usually need to build skills in training others and leading a team.
tips: Look inside the Postal Service first: Postmasters and Mail Superintendents earn $96,660, which is 60% more.
Transportation Security Screeners earn $66,770, or 10% more, and value the public service you already do.
Keep your driving record clean; most transport matches check it before they hire.

faq.q: What jobs can former mail carriers do?
faq.a: The closest matches are transit and intercity bus drivers (69%), Flight Attendants (67%) and Transportation Security Screeners (66%), based on O*NET 31.0. Light Truck Drivers are also 66% matched, but earn $44,860, which is 26% less than the $60,550 carrier median.

faq.q: Which careers for mail carriers pay more?
faq.a: 9 of the 25 matches pay more than carrying mail. Postmasters and Mail Superintendents earn $96,660 (60% more), Subway and Streetcar Operators $86,380 (43% more) and Railroad Conductors and Yardmasters $78,000 (29% more), according to BLS May 2025 data.

faq.q: Do mail carriers need more education to switch?
faq.a: Rarely. 20 of the 25 matches need no more education than carriers already have, including all of the top 10. In the closest match, 84% of workers have a high school diploma or the equivalent, and training is done on the job.

faq.q: What skills should mail carriers build?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are instructing, managing people, troubleshooting and equipment maintenance. Coordination already rates 2.75 out of 5 for carriers in O*NET, so the best-paid moves usually come from supervising others or learning to maintain vehicles and machines.
